\chapter{Have, and Count}
\label{ch:zh-you-ge}
\hlchaptermodality{24}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I have, say that there is something, and put a number against a noun with a measure word between them.}

Nine strokes across two characters give the numerals something to count at last, and \zh{个} is three strokes of which two are \zh{人}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[yǒu]{\zh{有} — six strokes, and a moon underneath}

\label{lesson:ZH-W24-you}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and its first character is a verb the book has gone twenty-three chapters without.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ de shū — kàn shū de rén} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{de} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hǎo bu hǎo} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ma — nǐ hǎo ma — shì ma — hǎo bu hǎo} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zhōngwén} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tóngxué} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — two strokes on top, \zh{月} beneath}
\begin{quote}
\zh{有}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Six strokes.} Two cross at the top; the remaining four build \zh{月}, the moon, underneath.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héng} across the top, left to right
  \item the long \textbf{piě} from the top centre, falling to the lower left and running past everything below it
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Horizontal before left-falling.} You have written that order twice already, in \zh{大} and in \zh{六}, and it decides these two.

Then \zh{月}:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{shù} down the left side
  \item the \textbf{héngzhégōu} across the top and down the right side, hooking left at the base — one stroke, two turns, no lift
  \item the upper \textbf{héng} inside it
  \item the lower \textbf{héng} inside it
\end{enumerate}

Enclose, then fill: the two inner bars come after the walls, exactly as in \zh{白} and \zh{百} and \zh{四}.

\textbf{One thing to watch.} Stroke 2 is the longest in the character and it must reach the bottom-left corner, well past \zh{月}. A short one turns \zh{有} into something that is not \zh{有}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{有} — bar, long fall, then \zh{月}'s four
  \item \emph{Cover:} write it again, and check the long stroke reaches the corner
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{有} have? (\textbf{Six}.) Which comes first, the horizontal or the falling stroke? (\textbf{The horizontal} — as in \zh{大} and \zh{六}.) What sits underneath? (\textbf{\zh{月}}, built walls-first.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E6\%9C\%89.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{有}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yǒu]{\zh{有} — to have, and there is}

\label{lesson:ZH-C24-you}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and the character is already yours.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǒu} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{de} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{liù} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{liù} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{xiǎo} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{有}} \emph{yǒu} is \textbf{third tone} — the dip, low and creaky, the same shape as the \zh{好} you have said since your first day and the \zh{五} you count with.

Say them in a row and only the mouth changes: \textbf{hǎo, wǔ, yǒu.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我有书}} \emph{wǒ yǒu shū} — I have a book. \textbf{\zh{我有名字}} — I have a name.
\end{quote}
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same verb says there is}]
\zh{有} is also how Mandarin says \textbf{there is} and \textbf{there are}. It is one verb doing both jobs, and no extra word is needed for the second:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{有人}} \emph{yǒu rén} — there is somebody. / somebody's here. \textbf{\zh{有中国人}} — there are Chinese people here.
\end{quote}

English needs \emph{have} for the first job and \emph{there is} for the second; Spanish needs \emph{tener} and \emph{hay}. Mandarin needs \zh{有}.

\textbf{And now the exception that every Mandarin course states early}, because it is the only one of its kind:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{有} is the one verb \zh{不} cannot negate.}
\end{quote}

\zh{不} has negated everything in this book so far — \zh{不好}, \zh{不是}, \zh{不谢} — and it cannot negate this. The negative of \zh{有} is \emph{méi yǒu}, said with a different negator altogether, whose character this book has not yet taught. Hold the rule now and the writing later: \textbf{\zh{不有} is never Mandarin.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hǎo, wǔ, yǒu} — three dips
  \item \zh{我有书} \zh{我有名字}
  \item \zh{有人}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tone is \zh{有}? (\textbf{Third}, the dip.) What are its two jobs? (\textbf{To have}, and \textbf{there is}.) Which negator does it refuse? (\textbf{\zh{不}} — \zh{有} takes \emph{méi} instead.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gè]{\zh{个} — three strokes, and you already write two of them}

\label{lesson:ZH-W24-ge}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons in, and this character is nearly free.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǒu} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn shū de rén} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{qī} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{qī} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zhōngguó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dà — dàjiā — xué — xuésheng — dàxué — dàxuésheng} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — \zh{人}, and a line under it}
\begin{quote}
\zh{个}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Three strokes}, and the first two are a character you have written since the opening chapter.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{piě}, falling from the peak to the lower left
  \item the \textbf{nà}, falling from the same peak to the lower right
  \item the \textbf{shù}, straight down from under the junction
\end{enumerate}

Strokes 1 and 2 are \textbf{\zh{人}} — the same pair, from the same peak, in the same order. All that is new is a vertical hung beneath it.

Keep the roof wide and the vertical dead centre. If the roof narrows, \zh{个} starts to look like \zh{人} with an accident underneath.

This is the cheapest character in the chapter and it does the most work in the one after it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{人} — then \zh{个}, which is \zh{人} with a line under it
  \item \emph{Cover:} write \zh{个} from memory
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{个} have? (\textbf{Three}.) Which character are the first two? (\textbf{\zh{人}}.) And the third? (\textbf{A vertical, straight down from the junction}.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E4\%B8\%AA.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{个}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gè]{\zh{个} — the word that goes between a number and a thing}

\label{lesson:ZH-C24-ge}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and this is what the numerals were for.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gè} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Hànyǔ, wǒ kàn shū} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bā} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bā} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{guó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dàxuésheng} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: number + \zh{个} + noun}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{In Mandarin a number cannot touch a noun. Something has to stand between them, and \zh{个} is the one that fits almost everything.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wrong:} \zh{三人} \textbf{Right:} \textbf{\zh{三个人}} \emph{sān ge rén} — three people \textbf{Right:} \textbf{\zh{一个学生}} \emph{yí ge xuésheng} — one student \textbf{Right:} \textbf{\zh{五个名字}} — five names
\end{quote}

You have been able to count to ninety-nine since the last chapter and there has been nothing to count. This is the missing piece, and it is one character.

English does this in a few places and does not notice: \emph{three \textbf{head} of cattle}, \emph{two \textbf{slices} of bread}, \emph{a \textbf{pair} of trousers}. Mandarin does it \textbf{every time}, for every noun, without exception.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{个}} is \emph{gè}, \textbf{fourth tone} — the sharp fall, the same shape as \zh{四} and \zh{六}.

But in the middle of a count it usually goes \textbf{light and toneless}: \emph{sān ge rén}, not \emph{sān gè rén}. It behaves the way \zh{吗} and \zh{的} do — a small word leaning on its neighbours.

And one sandhi you already own comes back here. \zh{一} is first tone alone, and before a fourth-tone syllable it rises: \textbf{\zh{一个}} is \emph{yí ge}, not \emph{yī ge}. That is the same tone change the hundred lesson taught on \zh{一百}.

Mandarin has dozens of measure words, each tied to a shape or a kind of thing, and \zh{个} is the general-purpose one. Use \zh{个} when you do not know which is right, and you will be understood every time.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sān ge rén} — \zh{三个人}
  \item \emph{yí ge xuésheng} — \zh{一个学生}
  \item \zh{五个名字}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What has to stand between a number and a noun? (\textbf{A measure word} — \zh{个} fits almost everything.) What is wrong with \zh{三人}? (\textbf{Nothing stands between the number and the noun}.) How is \zh{一个} said? (\emph{\textbf{Yí ge}} — \zh{一} rises before a fourth tone.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{我有一个名字}}

\label{lesson:ZH-C24-practice}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes with the sentence its two characters were for.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gè} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ de shū — kàn shū de rén} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{jiǔ} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{jiǔ} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{guó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dàxué} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — have, and count}]
Two characters this chapter, nine strokes between them, and here is the sentence they buy:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我有一个名字}} \emph{wǒ yǒu yí ge míngzi} — I have a name.
\end{quote}

Everything in it except \zh{有} and \zh{个} was already yours: \zh{我} from the chapter where you said who you were, \zh{一} from the counting chapter, \zh{名字} from the naming one. The chapter did not add a sentence; it added the two words that let the sentence exist.

And the same nine strokes give:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{有人}} — there is somebody. \textbf{\zh{三个学生}} — three students. \textbf{\zh{我有一个中国名字}} — I have a Chinese name.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Listen.} \emph{Wǒ yǒu yí ge míngzi. Yǒu rén. Sān ge xuésheng.}

\textbf{Speak.} Say what you have; then count three of something.

\textbf{Read.} \zh{我有一个名字} — \zh{有人} — \zh{三个学生}

\textbf{Write.} \zh{有} — bar, long fall, \zh{月}. \zh{个} — \zh{人}, then a line.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{我有一个名字}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{有人} \zh{三个学生}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{有} \zh{个}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I have a name.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\zh{我有一个名字}}.) What does \zh{有} do besides \emph{have}? (\textbf{It says \emph{there is}}.) And why can \zh{三} not sit straight against \zh{人}? (\textbf{A number needs a measure word} — \zh{三个人}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
